title: Clare
hook: Francis's friend who founded the Poor Clares and, tradition says, faced down soldiers holding the sacrament

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis greeted death with one word, welcome, and your line was sister death.

Soldiers are coming over the wall of a small convent outside Assisi. Inside are women with no weapons, and their abbess is sick in bed. Here's what the old account says she does. She has herself carried to the door. She asks for the sacrament, the consecrated bread kept in a small box, to be set in front of her. She bows down before it and prays. And the soldiers, the story says, turn back and leave. The woman at the door is Clare, Francis's friend, whose sisters came to be called the Poor Clares.

Clare grew up in a noble family in Assisi, Francis's town. She heard him preach and wanted the life he lived: poor, simple, given to God. The Legend of Saint Clare says she slipped out of her family's house at night and went to Francis and his brothers, who cut her hair as a sign she was leaving the old life behind. When her relatives came to drag her home, she held onto the altar and showed them her shorn head, and they let her be. She settled at a little church called San Damiano, and other women came, her own sister among them. Their life was enclosed, prayerful and poor, and for years Clare asked church leaders to let her sisters own nothing at all. Back to the door. In some tellings, as she prays before the sacrament, a voice answers that God will always guard them. Whatever you make of it, the story says something about Clare: her defense was not a wall or a sword, but stillness and prayer before what she held most holy. Catholics and other Christians honor her as a saint. The same Legend tells of her last days. Lying ill, she speaks to her own soul: go forth in peace, for you will have a good escort. The woman who walked out of her father's house at night ends by sending her soul out the door, without fear.
screen: `OUT OF HER FATHER'S HOUSE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Stand in a doorway, any door, feet on the floor and hands loose, and breathe. Think of what comes through doorways in your life, news, people, worry, and neither block it nor rush out to meet it. If you pray, hold in mind someone facing something frightening today; if not, let the breath slow and the doorframe hold you up.
Clare. Francis's friend, who left home at night for a poor life, led the sisters at San Damiano, and, the story says, met soldiers at the door with prayer.
Your line: go forth in peace. Clare said it to her own soul, without fear. Day eight hundred eighteen, done.

howItsDone: The Poor Clares live an enclosed life of prayer in convents around the world, and Catholics and some Anglicans keep a feast day for Saint Clare.

chat.says: Who was Clare of Assisi? I only really know the name.
options: She left home at night for a poor life, led the sisters at San Damiano, and met danger with prayer.
She was a wealthy noblewoman who gave her palace to Francis's friars and stayed at court.
She was Francis's teacher, who trained him to preach before he gathered his brothers.
chat.meaning: Clare left a noble home for poverty, led the enclosed sisters at San Damiano, and met the soldiers with stillness and prayer.

sources.ref: The Legend of Saint Clare (attributed to Thomas of Celano): her flight from home, the soldiers at San Damiano, her last words

notes: All Clare narrative is paraphrased from the Legend of Saint Clare; confirm each beat (night flight, hair cut at the Portiuncula, clinging to the altar, the attack on San Damiano, the voice, her words to her soul). The soldiers' identity (in Frederick II's army) is left out on purpose.

Her last words are given as 'Go forth in peace, for you have followed a good road', to match the index carry. Translations vary ('go forth without fear', 'you have a good escort'); confirm the paraphrase is fair.
'Her own sister' joining her: Agnes of Assisi. Confirm.
'Asking church leaders to let her sisters own nothing at all' refers to the privilege of poverty; no dates given. Confirm.
'Catholics and other Christians honor her as a saint' and howItsDone 'some Anglicans': confirm phrasing under the claims rule.
Index hook says 'founded the Poor Clares'; the script says her sisters 'came to be called the Poor Clares'. Confirm.
